Thought: Let me analyze each option to determine which characteristic of ethers makes them particularly dangerous fire hazards:

A. Formation of unstable peroxides - Ethers can form peroxides upon exposure to air and light over time. These peroxides are unstable and can be explosive, especially when concentrated during distillation or evaporation.

B. Low flash point and wide flammability range - Ethers typically have low flash points (the temperature at which they can form an ignitable mixture with air) and can burn across a wide range of concentrations in air. For example, diethyl ether has a flash point of about -45°C, making it extremely flammable at room temperature.

C. Reaction with oxidizing agents - While ethers can react with strong oxidizing agents, this is not their primary fire hazard characteristic.

D. Toxic combustion products - While combustion of any organic compound can produce toxic products, this is not the distinctive characteristic that makes ethers particularly dangerous fire hazards.

Based on my knowledge of chemistry, option B is correct. The extremely low flash points of many ethers combined with their wide flammability ranges (the range of concentrations in air at which they can ignite) is what makes them particularly dangerous fire hazards. This means they can easily form flammable vapors at room temperature and ignite with minimal ignition energy.
Final Answer: [ANSWER]B[/ANSWER]
